transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A major telecommunications company has announced plans to provide free high-speed internet access to every public school in the country over the next three years. The initiative, which will cost an estimated two billion dollars, aims to close the digital divide by ensuring that students in low-income areas have the same access to online educational resources as their wealthier peers. Company executives say the program will also provide free Wi-Fi in public housing complexes and community centers in underserved neighborhoods. Education experts have praised the announcement, noting that millions of students currently lack reliable internet access at home, putting them at a significant disadvantage for completing homework and developing digital skills essential for the modern workforce. The program is expected to benefit approximately 12 million students across 20,000 schools. The federal government has also pledged to contribute additional funding to help schools purchase devices and train teachers to effectively integrate technology into their classrooms.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.

2. What do education experts say about internet access for students?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: Scientists in Japan have developed a new type of wearable robotic suit that can help elderly people and individuals with mobility impairments walk more easily. The device, which weighs just under five kilograms, uses small motors and sensors to detect the wearer's movements and provide assistance to the legs and hips. In clinical trials involving 120 participants with walking difficulties, users reported a 40 percent reduction in the effort required to walk and significantly less pain in their knees and hips. The suit can be adjusted to provide different levels of assistance depending on the user's needs, and it can be worn under regular clothing. Researchers say the technology could help millions of older adults maintain their independence and reduce the risk of falls, which are a leading cause of injury and hospitalization among elderly populations. The company that developed the suit plans to begin selling it to hospitals and rehabilitation centers next year, with a consumer version available within two years at an expected cost of around 3,000 dollars.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Male)
paras: A new international study has found that people who regularly eat meals prepared at home have a significantly lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared to those who frequently eat at restaurants or rely on pre-packaged meals. The research, which followed more than 50,000 adults over a period of ten years, found that individuals who cooked at home five or more times per week had a 28 percent lower risk of developing the disease. Researchers say the difference is likely due to several factors: home-cooked meals typically contain less salt, sugar, and unhealthy fats than restaurant meals, and people who cook at home tend to eat more vegetables and whole grains. The study also found that home cooks generally have better overall diets regardless of their income level or cooking skill. Public health officials say the findings highlight the importance of teaching basic cooking skills in schools and making healthy, affordable ingredients more accessible in low-income neighborhoods where fast food restaurants are often concentrated.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.

7. According to researchers, why do home-cooked meals have health benefits?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Man (Justin): Hey, Megan. Are you going to the student government meeting tonight? They're talking about the proposal to build a new student center on campus.

Woman (Megan): I heard about that, but I'm not sure if I can make it. I have a chemistry exam tomorrow that I really need to study for. What's the proposal about exactly? I thought the current student center was fine.

Man: Well, the current one is really small and outdated. They're planning to build a much larger facility with a new cafeteria, more study spaces, a game room, a movie theater, and even a fitness center. It would also include new offices for all the student clubs and organizations.
Woman: That sounds great, but how are they planning to pay for it? I hope they're not going to raise tuition again—they already increased it by five percent this year.

Man: That's the big debate tonight. The university is proposing a small student fee increase—about 75 dollars per semester—to help cover the costs. They say it's a good investment because the new center would improve campus life for everyone. But a lot of students are against it, saying they can't afford any additional fees.

Woman: Seventy-five dollars a semester does add up. That's an extra 150 dollars a year. I'm already working two part-time jobs just to pay for textbooks and groceries. Another fee would be really difficult for me.

Man: I know what you mean. But the other side says that if we don't approve the fee now, construction costs will only go up in the future, and we might never get a new student center. They're also talking about creating more than 200 part-time jobs for students at the new center.

Woman: Hmm, that is a good point about jobs. But I still think they should look for other ways to fund it—maybe from alumni donations or corporate sponsorships? Why should students have to bear the entire cost?

Man: Actually, the university is contributing about 60 percent of the total cost from their endowment. The student fee would cover the remaining 40 percent. And the fee wouldn't start until construction is finished, which would be in three years. None of us would have to pay it until we've already graduated, technically.

Woman: Wait, really? So current students would be voting on a fee that we wouldn't even have to pay ourselves? That changes things a bit. But it still doesn't seem fair to pass the cost on to future students.

Man: Well, that's what student government is for—we get to decide whether it's worth it for the future of the campus. I think I'm going to vote in favor of it, even though I'll never get to use the new center. The university has needed a better student space for decades.
Woman: You might be right. I still wish I could make it to the meeting to hear more of the discussion, but I really have to study for this exam. Let me know what they decide, okay?
Man: Sure thing. I'll take notes and text you after the meeting. Good luck on your chemistry test!
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. Why is Megan hesitant to support the student fee increase?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Grace): Hello, is this the campus housing office? I'm calling because I have a problem with my dorm room.
Man (Officer): Yes, this is the housing office. My name is Robert. How can I help you today?

Woman: Well, I live in Room 312 in Maple Hall, and there's a leak in the ceiling above my bed. It started dripping yesterday during the rainstorm, and now my mattress and some of my books are wet. I'm really worried it's going to get worse, and there's also mold starting to appear on the wall.
Man: I'm sorry to hear that—that sounds really frustrating. Have you reported this to your resident assistant yet? That's usually the first step for maintenance requests.

Woman: I tried to find my RA yesterday, but she wasn't in her room, and she hasn't responded to my text messages. It's been over 24 hours now, and the leak seems to be getting worse every time it rains. I don't know what else to do.

Man: I understand. Let me check our system to see if a work order has been submitted already... No, I don't see anything for your room. I'll put in an emergency maintenance request right away, and we should be able to send someone to look at it today or tomorrow at the latest.

Woman: Thank you so much. But in the meantime, is there anything I can do about the water? I've put a bucket under the drip, but the carpet is getting wet too. Also, I can't really sleep in my bed right now because the mattress is soaked.

Man: I can arrange for you to stay in a temporary room in another building for a couple of nights while we make repairs. Would that work for you? We have some guest rooms available in Oak Hall, which is just across the quad.
Woman: That would be wonderful, thank you. But what about my belongings? I don't want to leave my books and computer in a room with a leak and mold.

Man: You can move your important items to the temporary room. The maintenance team will also bring in fans to dry out the carpet and treat the mold as soon as they arrive. I'll make a note that this is an urgent situation.
Woman: Great. When can I pick up the key for the temporary room?

Man: You can come to the housing office anytime before 5 PM today to pick up the key. Just bring your student ID with you. I'll also give you a voucher for the campus laundry so you can wash any bedding or clothing that got wet.
Woman: I really appreciate your help with this, Robert. I was starting to panic a little bit.

Man: No problem at all—that's what we're here for. I'll follow up with maintenance first thing to make sure they prioritize your room. And if you don't hear from someone within a few hours, please call us back.
Woman: I will do that. Thank you again so much.

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: The Olympic Games are the world's largest and most prestigious international sporting event, bringing together thousands of athletes from more than 200 countries to compete in a wide range of sports. The modern Olympics were first held in Athens, Greece, in 1896, inspired by the ancient Olympic Games that took place in Olympia, Greece, for over a thousand years from the 8th century BCE to the 4th century CE. Today, the Games are held every two years, alternating between the Summer Olympics and Winter Olympics, with cities from around the world bidding years in advance to host the event.

Hosting the Olympics is an enormous undertaking that requires years of preparation and billions of dollars in investment. Host cities typically build new stadiums, athletes' villages, transportation infrastructure, and security facilities to accommodate the games. While hosting the Olympics can bring significant benefits—including international prestige, improved infrastructure, increased tourism, and a boost to the local economy—it also presents major challenges. The high costs of construction, security, and operations often leave host cities with large debts that take decades to repay, and many purpose-built venues fall into disuse after the games end. In recent years, there has been growing interest in making the Olympics more sustainable and affordable by using existing facilities where possible and encouraging host cities to develop long-term plans for venue use after the games.

The Olympics have also played an important role in social and political history. The Games have been used as a platform for political protest, such as when American athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised their fists in a black power salute during the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, and when multiple countries boycotted the 1980 Moscow Games and 1984 Los Angeles Games during the Cold War. More recently, the Olympics have become more inclusive, with the addition of new sports such as skateboarding, sport climbing, and surfing to attract younger audiences, and increased participation by female athletes—women now make up nearly half of all Olympic competitors, compared to just over 20 percent in 1960. Despite the controversies and challenges, the Olympics remain a powerful symbol of international cooperation and human achievement, inspiring millions of people around the world.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Walking is one of the simplest and most accessible forms of exercise, yet its health benefits are often underestimated compared to more intense forms of physical activity like running or going to the gym. Research has consistently shown that regular walking can have a profound impact on both physical and mental health, and it has the advantage of being free, requiring no special equipment, and being easy for most people to incorporate into their daily routines.

One of the most well-documented benefits of walking is its positive effect on cardiovascular health. Studies following hundreds of thousands of people have found that regular walkers have a significantly lower risk of heart disease, high blood pressure, and stroke compared to people who are sedentary. Walking just 30 minutes a day, five days a week, can reduce the risk of heart disease by approximately 20 percent, according to the World Health Organization. Unlike high-impact exercises like running, walking is gentle on the joints, making it an ideal form of exercise for people of all ages and fitness levels, including older adults and those recovering from injuries.

Walking also has important benefits for mental health and cognitive function. Research has shown that going for a walk, particularly in natural environments like parks or woodlands, can reduce stress, anxiety, and symptoms of depression. Walking increases blood flow to the brain and stimulates the production of endorphins, the body's natural feel-good chemicals. Studies have also found that walking can improve creativity and problem-solving abilities—many people report that they get their best ideas while going for a walk. Some companies have even started holding walking meetings, where participants discuss business while strolling outside, leading to more creative thinking and more engaged discussions.

Weight management is another benefit of regular walking. While it may not burn calories as quickly as more intense exercises, walking regularly can help people maintain a healthy weight by burning calories, boosting metabolism, and reducing cravings for sugary snacks. A brisk 30-minute walk burns approximately 150 calories, which adds up significantly over time. Walking after meals has been shown to be particularly effective for controlling blood sugar levels, which is especially important for people at risk of diabetes.

Experts recommend aiming for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity walking per week, which works out to about 30 minutes a day, five days a week. This doesn't have to be done all at once—three ten-minute walks throughout the day provide the same health benefits as one continuous 30-minute walk. Simple changes like taking the stairs instead of the elevator, parking farther away from store entrances, or getting off the bus one stop early can help people fit more walking into their days without setting aside dedicated time for exercise.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: The concept of a universal basic income, or UBI, has been debated by economists, politicians, and social thinkers for centuries, but it has gained significant mainstream attention in recent years amid concerns about automation, rising inequality, and the changing nature of work. Universal basic income is a system in which all citizens of a country receive a regular, unconditional sum of money from the government, regardless of their employment status, income level, or any other eligibility requirements. Unlike traditional welfare programs, which typically have strict qualification criteria and require recipients to demonstrate need, UBI would be given to everyone, from the poorest to the wealthiest members of society.

Supporters of UBI argue that it would provide a financial safety net for all citizens, ensuring that everyone has enough money to meet their basic needs for food, shelter, and clothing, even in times of economic disruption. They point to the potential for automation to replace millions of jobs in the coming decades, from driving and retail to many white-collar positions, arguing that UBI could help people transition as the job market changes. Supporters also believe that UBI would simplify the complex welfare system, reduce administrative costs, and give people more freedom to pursue education, care for family members, start businesses, or do volunteer work without the pressure of having to take any available job just to survive. Several small-scale experiments with UBI have been conducted in countries around the world, including Finland, Canada, and Kenya, with many reporting positive results such as improved well-being, reduced stress, and increased employment rates in some cases.

However, critics of UBI raise several important concerns. One of the most common objections is cost—providing every citizen with a basic income would be extremely expensive, requiring significant tax increases that could discourage work and investment. Critics also worry that an unconditional income might reduce some people's incentive to work, leading to labor shortages and reduced economic productivity. They argue that targeted welfare programs are more efficient because they direct resources specifically to those who need them most, rather than giving money to wealthy people who don't need it. Some also question whether a basic income would be enough to cover people's needs in expensive areas, or whether it might lead to inflation as people have more money to spend.

While a full national UBI has not yet been implemented in any country, the debate continues as more places experiment with the idea and as the future of work remains uncertain. Some proponents have also proposed partial forms of UBI, such as guaranteed income for specific groups like parents or young adults, as more politically feasible first steps.

24. What is one argument made by supporters of UBI?
